Solitude (The Mulatress)

Biography

The history of the Caribbean is inscribed with the epic struggles of men and women who defied the crushing brutality of chattel slavery to assert their humanity and demand absolute freedom. Among the most legendary and revered figures of this relentless resistance is La Mulâtresse Solitude, known simply as Solitude. A heroic Guadeloupean freedom fighter, her fierce participation in the 1802 insurrection against the reintroduction of slavery ordered by First Consul Napoleon Bonaparte has immortalized her as a timeless symbol of women's leadership, courage, and unyielding defiance against colonial tyranny. Fighting alongside legendary revolutionary commanders such as Louis Delgrès and Joseph Ignace, Solitude chose the perils of armed resistance over submission, embodying the immortal revolutionary slogan of the Guadeloupean insurgents: Vivre libre ou mourir (Live free or die).

Early Life and the Brutality of the Code Noir

Born around 1772 in the French Caribbean colony of Guadeloupe, the woman who would later be immortalized as Solitude entered a world strictly governed by the dehumanizing mandates of the Code Noir. Historical traditions record that she was originally named Rosalie, the daughter of an enslaved African woman who endured the horrors of the Middle Passage or coastal captivity, and a French sailor who sexually assaulted her. As a mulâtresse (a person of mixed African and European heritage born into slavery), her early existence was marked by profound alienation and violence. Under colonial law, the child followed the status of the mother, condemning young Rosalie to the relentless exploitation of the plantation economy.

Growing up surrounded by the cane fields of Basse-Terre, Rosalie bore witness to the daily atrocities inflicted upon enslaved laborers by white planters and overseers. The plantation hierarchy was designed to crush the human spirit through physical torture, forced labor, and social fragmentation. Yet, even within the suffocating confines of bondage, enslaved populations cultivated rich networks of cultural survival and covert resistance. Inspired by news of slave revolts across the Caribbean—most notably the explosive beginnings of the Haitian Revolution led by figures like Toussaint Louverture—Rosalie developed an acute consciousness of liberation. It was during these formative years of internal resistance that she began to distance herself from the colonial structures, eventually adopting the name "Solitude"—a testament to her fierce independence, spiritual fortitude, and self-reliance in a world determined to subjugate her.

The First Abolition of Slavery in 1794

The revolutionary fervor sweeping through mainland France following 1789 inevitably sent seismic shockwaves across the Atlantic colonies. In February 1794, the French National Convention officially decreed the abolition of slavery throughout all French territories. Shortly thereafter, the revolutionary commissioner Victor Hugues arrived in Guadeloupe with a fleet and a small force, carrying the decree of freedom and rallying the newly emancipated Black and mixed-race population to drive out the occupying British forces who had been invited by royalist white planters to preserve the slave economy.

For the first time in her life, Solitude experienced the sweet taste of liberty. The period between 1794 and 1802 transformed Guadeloupean society. Emancipatees established smallholdings, integrated into the local defense forces, and reveled in their status as free citizens. Solitude reportedly joined a community of Maroons and independent cultivators in the lush, mountainous interior of Basse-Terre. Here, amidst the volcanic valleys and dense tropical forests, free Black men and women built self-sustaining agricultural communities governed by their own social norms, fiercely protective of their hard-won autonomy.

"To have known the sweetness of freedom after the bitterness of chains makes the thought of returning to bondage a fate worse than death itself. We stand upon this soil not as property, but as sovereign children of liberty."

Napoleon Bonaparte's Betrayal and the 1802 Invasion

The dawn of freedom, however, was tragically brief. By 1799, Napoleon Bonaparte had seized power in France as First Consul. Driven by imperial ambitions and heavily influenced by the colonial planting lobby, Napoleon sought to restore French economic dominance in the Americas by re-establishing the lucrative plantation system. Following the Treaty of Amiens in early 1802, which brought a temporary peace with Great Britain, Napoleon enacted the Law of 20 May 1802, officially restoring slavery and the slave trade in colonies where it had not been successfully enforced, while secretly ordering military expeditions to crush Black authority in Saint-Domingue (Haiti) and Guadeloupe.

In May 1802, a formidable French expeditionary force consisting of 3,400 heavily armed troops commanded by General Antoine Richepance arrived in the waters of Guadeloupe. Richepance's orders were ruthless: disarm all Black and mixed-race soldiers, purge the military leadership, and return the Black population to plantation servitude. While some colonial officers, such as Magloire Pélage, chose compliance or capitulation, a valiant core of revolutionary officers refused to surrender their freedom. Led by the charismatic colonel Louis Delgrès and the fearless captain Joseph Ignace, the insurgents issued a resounding call to arms, publishing a historic proclamation to the universe declaring their intention to fight to the death to preserve their liberty.

The Battle for Liberty: Solitude in the Insurrection

When the call to defend freedom echoed across the valleys of Guadeloupe, Solitude did not hesitate. Although she was several months pregnant at the time, she answered the summons of Louis Delgrès and rallied to the insurgent camps at Dolé and Fort Saint-Charles. In doing so, she became one of the most prominent female combatants in the anti-slavery war, transforming from an independent rural cultivator into a frontline revolutionary soldier.

Historical accounts and oral traditions describe Solitude fighting with astonishing ferocity alongside male insurgents. Wielding a machete and a musket, she engaged French colonial troops in desperate skirmishes through the rugged terrain of Basse-Terre. Her presence on the battlefield served as a powerful moral force; she rallied the fighters, tended to the wounded, and exhorted her comrades to give no quarter to the invaders who sought to re-enslave them and their unborn children. Her heroism shattered traditional colonial gender dynamics, proving that women were vital pillars of revolutionary warfare.

"Live free or die! We prefer death to the chains of slavery, and our blood shall nourish the soil of liberty for generations unborn."

Capture, Execution, and the Martyrdom of Matouba

Despite their overwhelming courage and tactical brilliance, the Guadeloupean insurgents were eventually outnumbered and outgunned by Richepance's well-supplied reinforcements. By late May 1802, insurgent forces had been pushed back into their mountain strongholds. On May 28, 1802, surrounded at the habitation D'Anglemont in Matouba on the slopes of the Soufrière volcano, Louis Delgrès and approximately 400 of his followers made a legendary sacrifice. Rather than face capture and re-enslavement, they ignited their gunpowder stores, blowing themselves up and taking hundreds of advancing French soldiers with them in a defiant final explosion of liberty.

Solitude was captured around the time of the fall of Matouba, wounded but surviving the carnage. Recognized as a prominent leader among the rebels, she was thrown into a colonial prison and sentenced to death by military tribunal. However, in a display of cold, economic calculation, French colonial authorities stayed her execution because of her advanced pregnancy. Under the restored laws of slavery, the unborn child represented valuable property to the colonial state. Solitude spent her final months in a damp cell, carrying her child to term under the shadow of the gallows.

On November 28, 1802, Solitude gave birth to her child. Just one day later, on November 29, 1802, with her bodily utility to the slave system fulfilled, the colonial authorities brought her to the scaffold. At approximately 30 years of age, La Mulâtresse Solitude was hanged. Her newborn child was immediately consigned to slavery, entering the world handcuffed by the very system its mother had died fighting to destroy.

Historical Legacy and Cultural Immortality

For over a century, official colonial histories attempted to erase or minimize the heroic resistance of Solitude and the 1802 insurgents. Yet, her memory survived in the rich oral traditions of the Guadeloupean people and in brief notations in 19th-century historical accounts by writers such as Auguste Lacour. In 1972, her global legacy was permanently cemented with the publication of André Schwarz-Bart's landmark novel, La Mulâtresse Solitude, which wove historical facts with poetic resonance to present her story to the world.

Today, Solitude stands venerated as a foundational matriarch of Caribbean freedom. Her sacrifices are commemorated through public monuments across the francophone world, including the striking statue sculpted by Jacky Poulier erected in Les Abymes, Guadeloupe, in 1999, and a monument inaugurated in the Jardin Solitude in Paris in 2022—making her the first Black woman honored with a statue in the French capital. Solitude's life remains an eternal beacon of resilience, reminding future generations that the liberation of the Caribbean was forged through the unflinching courage of women who dared to defy empire.

Major Contributions

  • Solitude's most profound historical contribution lies in her fearless military leadership and frontline participation in the 1802 Guadeloupean insurrection against Napoleon Bonaparte's reintroduction of slavery.
  • By taking up arms alongside revolutionary commanders Louis Delgrès and Joseph Ignace while heavily pregnant, she shattered colonial gender paradigms and demonstrated that women were indispensable catalysts in armed struggle against racial oppression and chattel slavery.
  • Beyond her immediate military heroism, Solitude made an enduring ideological contribution to Afro-Caribbean feminism and historical consciousness.
  • Her willingness to face the scaffold rather than accept re-enslavement provided an enduring moral framework for anti-colonial resistance across the Caribbean.
  • Today, she serves as a permanent symbol of dignity and human rights, inspiring global educational, artistic, and political movements that seek to reclaim enslaved women's narratives and celebrate their foundational roles in shaping modern concepts of universal liberty.
